title: The Fathers at Work
subtitle: The councils wrote the creeds, but the doctrine was carried between the meetings, in exiles, letters, famine relief, and one long fight over grace. The people who did the work.

sections.title: Where Doctrine Actually Gets Made
sections.body:
The councils get the fame, and there is a distortion in that. A council is a few weeks of bishops in a hall. The doctrine it confirms is decades of work done somewhere else, in sermons preached to distracted congregations, in letters carried by hand across the sea, in books written in exile, in arguments between friends who loved each other and wounded each other. Nicaea met in 325 and confessed the Son to be fully God, and if the story ended there it would be tidy. It did not end there. For most of the next fifty years the Nicene confession was besieged, out of favor at court more often than not, its defenders deposed and banished while its opponents held the great churches. Jerome, looking back, wrote that the world groaned and marveled to find itself Arian.

What carried the truth across those decades was not an institution. It was people, a handful of them, stubborn and mortal and in most cases badly treated. It is worth watching how they worked, because the church in every age assumes its doctrine is kept safe by documents, and it never is. Documents are kept safe by people who will pay for them. The creed a congregation recites in ninety seconds on a Sunday morning was carried through the fourth century the way a child is carried through a war zone, at cost, by hands that shook. What follows is the account of some of those hands.

sections.title: Athanasius Against the World
sections.body:
Athanasius came to Nicaea as a young deacon from Alexandria, and three years later he became its bishop, and for the next forty-five years he was the argument. Five times he was driven from his city, exiled by four different emperors, seventeen years in all spent on the run or in hiding, some of it among the monks of the Egyptian desert who guarded him like one of their own. Councils packed against him deposed him. Imperial letters denounced him. At the lowest point it seemed that every power in the world, court and church together, had agreed to bury the Nicene confession, and the proverb that grew up around his name says the rest. Athanasius against the world.

What held him was not temperament, though he had one. His enemies called him violent and high-handed, and some modern historians partly agree, and we do not need him to be a gentle man for the story to be true. What held him was a single conviction he had written down when he was still young, in a small book called On the Incarnation. Only God can save. If the Son is a creature, however exalted, then the cross is a creature's death and we are still in our sins. Salvation itself, not a word in a creed, was what he refused to surrender. He outlived his emperors, died in his own bed in 373 with the fight still undecided, and was vindicated eight years later at Constantinople, a victory he never saw.

sections.title: Three Friends and a Sister
sections.body:
In the generation after Athanasius the work passed to Cappadocia, to one remarkable family and its friends. Basil of Caesarea was the organizer. When famine struck his region in 368 he preached the rich into opening their barns, and at the edge of his city he built a compound of hospital, hostel, and kitchen that contemporaries described as a new city for the poor. When the emperor's prefect threatened him with confiscation and death, Basil answered, as his friend told the story, that a man who owns nothing but books and worn clothes is a hard man to threaten. The same Basil wrote the treatise that secured the deity of the Holy Spirit, and the rules that still shape the monastic life of the East.

His friend Gregory of Nazianzus was the poet. Reluctant, easily wounded, half in love with solitude, he was talked into serving a tiny Nicene congregation in Arian Constantinople, and in 380 he preached there the five sermons on the Trinity that earned him the name the Theologian. His friendship with Basil broke, painfully, when Basil pressed him into a bishopric he did not want, and it never fully healed, and the doctrine got made anyway, by wounded friends rather than untroubled ones. Behind them stood Basil's household. His elder sister Macrina had claimed the life of prayer and poverty before any of her brothers, and their brother Gregory of Nyssa wrote of her, without embarrassment, as his teacher. When the council met at Constantinople in 381 to finish the creed, Gregory of Nyssa carried her teaching into the room.

sections.title: Augustine Against Pelagius
sections.body:
The last great fight of the era was not about who Christ is but about what his grace must do, and it began with a sentence in a prayer. In the Confessions Augustine had asked God, in effect, to give what you command and command what you will. A British ascetic in Rome named Pelagius heard the line quoted aloud and was appalled. To him it sounded like an excuse dressed as piety, a way for lax Christians to sigh that obedience was beyond them. Pelagius deserves his case stated fairly, because it was serious. God does not command the impossible. Human beings keep the freedom they were created with, sin is habit and imitation rather than a ruined nature, and grace comes as law, teaching, forgiveness, and the example of Christ. He was a moral reformer disgusted by a church going soft in its new respectability, and on that last point he was not wrong.

Augustine answered from his own biography. He had not been advised into holiness, he had been rescued, pulled out of a will that kept choosing its chains, and he knew the difference between instruction and deliverance. If Pelagius is right, grace is information, the cross is an illustration, and the strong save themselves. The church weighed the two accounts of the human condition and sided with Augustine, at Carthage in 418 and again at Ephesus in 431, though it did not follow him into every conclusion he drew late in life, and it has argued about predestination ever since. On the floor of it the church held. We do not climb to God. God descends.

sections.title: How the Work Was Done
sections.body:
Notice the shape of their working lives, because it corrects a modern assumption. None of these men did theology as a profession set apart from the church. Athanasius wrote on the run, between congregations and hiding places. Basil's treatise on the Spirit grew out of a dispute over the wording of the doxology his own people sang, which is to say the doctrine came out of worship and returned to it. Gregory preached his orations on the Trinity to a real congregation in a borrowed chapel, hecklers included. Augustine worked out the doctrine of grace while judging lawsuits, preaching several times a week, and answering letters from anxious strangers. In the same years Jerome sat in Bethlehem grinding the Scriptures out of Hebrew and Greek into the common Latin of the people. The instruments of the era were the sermon, the letter, the psalm, and the funeral. Doctrine was pastoral work done carefully, or it was nothing.

And it ran on friendship, which means it ran on the injuries of friendship. Basil and Gregory quarreled and half reconciled. Jerome and Augustine corresponded for years with a courtesy that kept curdling into suspicion. These were not serene sages. They were difficult men under pressure, loving God and irritating one another, and the church's most permanent sentences were forged in that heat. Anyone waiting for calm and unanimous experts before trusting a doctrine will wait forever. Truth in the church has usually traveled the way it did then, hand to hand, between people who could barely stand each other and would have died for each other.

sections.title: What We Owe Them
sections.body:
It is possible to finish this story ungratefully, and most generations have managed it. One kind of ingratitude treats the fathers as infallible oracles, quoting them the way they refused to quote anyone but Scripture. Another treats them as dead weight, the complicating ancestors a simpler faith should shed. Both refuse the actual inheritance, which is not a set of untouchable men but a set of tested sentences and a demonstration of what the sentences cost. The Nicene faith is not true because Athanasius suffered for it. But the suffering is evidence of something the modern church struggles to believe, that doctrine can matter enough to lose everything for, that the difference between begotten and made is the difference between being saved by God and being encouraged by a creature.

They also leave us an indictment we should not dodge. These people held together what we have divided. Basil built the hospital and parsed the Trinity, one life. Augustine wrote on grace at a depth no one has passed and catechized fishermen the same week. We have split that inheritance into specialties, doctrine for the academics, mercy for the activists, prayer for the mystics, and every specialty is thinner for the divorce. The fathers would not recognize the arrangement. Truth that feeds no one, and charity that believes nothing, would have looked to them like the two halves of a corpse. They worked as if the creed and the soup kitchen came from the same Lord. They do. That is the inheritance. We have mostly declined it.

keyFigures.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
keyFigures.note: Bishop exiled five times under four emperors for refusing to yield the Nicene confession.

keyFigures.name: Basil of Caesarea
keyFigures.note: Bishop and builder of the poor city at Caesarea, who secured the deity of the Spirit.

keyFigures.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
keyFigures.note: The reluctant preacher whose orations on the Trinity earned him the name the Theologian.

keyFigures.name: Gregory of Nyssa
keyFigures.note: Basil's brother, the contemplative mind of the family, present at Constantinople in 381.

keyFigures.name: Macrina the Younger
keyFigures.note: Elder sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who claimed the ascetic life first and taught them both.

keyFigures.name: Pelagius
keyFigures.note: British ascetic and moral reformer whose account of grace the church weighed and refused.

keyFigures.name: Augustine of Hippo
keyFigures.note: Bishop whose doctrine of rescuing grace the church affirmed at Carthage and Ephesus.
